text: Lesson 9 showed you where the Security log lives and how to filter it by Event ID. This lesson gives you the five IDs worth memorizing before you ever sit down in front of a real log — they show up in almost every logon investigation, account audit, and privilege question you'll face: 4624, 4625, 4672, 4720, and 4728.

4624 is a successful logon — the single most common Security-log event on any active machine. The field that turns it from noise into a lead is Logon Type: 2 is interactive at the keyboard, 3 is a network logon, 10 is RemoteInteractive, meaning RDP. 4625 is its failure twin. One 4625 is a fat-fingered password; a burst against the same account, or across many machines, is the signature of a brute-force attempt.

4672 fires whenever an account logs on with administrator-equivalent privileges — membership that carries rights like debugging processes or taking ownership of objects. It's not alarming by itself, since plenty of legitimate admin work triggers it every day, but a 4672 right after a 4624 for an account that shouldn't have admin rights at all is worth escalating immediately, not filing away.

4720 means a new user account was created on this system or domain — routine IT work on its own; what matters is who created it, when, and what happens to it next. 4728 means an account was added to a security-enabled global group, the kind of group that can carry real permissions across an entire domain. Neither event is alarming in isolation.

Watched together, though, they tell a different story: 4720 creates an account, 4728 adds it to a privileged group minutes later, and 4672 shows it logging on with elevated rights — a textbook pattern for an attacker or malicious insider quietly provisioning themselves persistent admin access. Next: Sysmon, for visibility these five IDs alone can't give you.
